As Sweden's special envoy in Budapest in 1944 he saved thousands of Jews with protective passports and "Swedish territory" safe houses, then vanished in 1945 after Soviet SMERSH agents detained him — who was this humanitarian diplomat?
Raoul Wallenberg: Swedish diplomat and humanitarian (1912–1945). Raoul Wallenberg (4 August 1912 – disappeared 17 January 1945) was a Swedish architect, businessman, diplomat, and humanitarian.
The longest-serving prime minister in Slovak history, he has led the country across four separate terms since founding his left-wing party in 1999 — who is he?
Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence and Avondale
Robert Fico: Prime Minister of Slovakia (2006–2010, 2012–2018, 2023–present)
After serving as Prime Minister of Kuwait from 1978 to 2006, this royal briefly became Emir for just nine days before abdicating — who is he?
Saad Al-Salim Al-Sabah: Emir of Kuwait in 2006.
Anointed by the prophet Samuel as the first king of a newly unified Israelite kingdom, he died falling on his own sword after defeat by the Philistines at Mount Gilboa — who was he?
Saul: Biblical figure and Israelite monarch.
Known by the kunya Abu Idris, this Chechen guerrilla commander helped recapture Grozny in 1996 and later masterminded some of Russia's worst hostage-taking attacks — who is he?

After revealing Zeus's abduction of a nymph to a river god and later cheating death itself, this mythical king of Corinth was condemned to forever push a boulder up a hill, only to watch it roll back down — who is he?
Sisyphus: King of Ephyra in Greek mythology.
This Indonesian general became his country's second president in 1967, two years after his troops put down an attempted coup — who is he?
Suharto: President of Indonesia from 1967 to 1998.
Built during Solomon's reign in the 10th century BCE and later rebuilt after the Babylonian exile, this sacred structure stood as the central place of Israelite worship in the Old City — what was it?
Temple in Jerusalem: Former places of Israelite and Jewish worship.
Born Joaquim José da Silva Xavier, this leader of Brazil's Inconfidência Mineira independence plot was hanged in 1792 and is now a national hero — by what one-word nickname is he remembered?
Tiradentes: 18th-century Brazilian revolutionary and national hero.

Formed after the Napoleonic Wars by fusing the old Dutch Republic, the Austrian-ruled Low Countries, and the Prince-Bishopric of Liège into a buffer state under William I of Orange-Nassau, this polity collapsed with the 1830 Belgian Revolution — what was it called?
United Kingdom of the Netherlands: European territory (1815–1839)

A protégé of murdered dissident Boris Nemtsov, this Russian-British activist and filmmaker has served as vice-chairman of an NGO founded by an exiled former oligarch, and received the Civil Courage Prize in 2018 after being repeatedly targeted for his opposition to the Kremlin. Who is he?
Who is this — “Female figure and also place of evil mentioned in the Book of Revelation”?
Whore of Babylon: Female figure and also place of evil mentioned in the Book of Revelation.

Founded by Modu Chanyu after overthrowing the Yuezhi, this nomadic tribal confederation dominated the eastern Eurasian steppe for centuries before a long conflict with the Han dynasty split it apart — what was this confederation called?
Xiongnu: Eurasian steppe confederation and empire. Modu Chanyu, the supreme leader after 209 BC, founded the Xiongnu Empire.

Once one of the nine members of China's most powerful decision-making body, this former security chief was arrested on corruption charges in 2014 after a career that began in the oil and gas industry — who is he?
Which one below was born first?
Joseph Schumpeter (born 1883) is the earliest of the four. Joseph Alois Schumpeter (German: [ˈʃʊmpeːtɐ]; February 8, 1883 – January 8, 1950) was an Austrian political economist.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Which of these people was born first?
Jīvaka (born 401 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four began earliest?
C++ (founded 1983) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these is an astronomer?
Which of these four is a mathematician?
Hugh Everett III is a mathematician. Hugh Everett III (November 11, 1930 – July 19, 1982) was an American physicist who proposed the relative state interpretation of quantum mechanics.
What is the atomic number of Silver?
Silver is a chemical element; it has symbol Ag (from Latin argentum 'silver') and atomic number 47.
What is the atomic number of Calcium?
Calcium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ca and atomic number 20.
In what year was Adrian Newey born?
Adrian Newey: Adrian Martin Newey (born 26 December 1958) is a British engineer, aerodynamicist, automotive designer, and motorsport executive.
In what year was Werner Heisenberg born?
Werner Heisenberg: Heisenberg published his Umdeutung paper in 1925, a major reinterpretation of old quantum theory.
In what year was Srinivasa Ramanujan born?
Srinivasa Ramanujan Iyengar (22 December 1887 – 26 April 1920) was an Indian mathematician who worked during the early 20th century.
In what year did Ted Kaczynski die?
Ted Kaczynski: The FBI used the case identifier UNABOM (University and Airline Bombing) before his identity was known, resulting in the media naming him the "Unabomber".
In what year did Ada Lovelace die?
Ada Lovelace: Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer.
In what year was Kepler's Supernova discovered?
Kepler's Supernova: SN 1604, also known as Kepler's Supernova, Kepler's Nova or Kepler's Star, was a Type Ia supernova that occurred in the Milky Way, in the constellation Ophiuchus.
PHP: Rasmus Lerdorf. PHP is a general-purpose scripting language geared towards web development.
Which company manufactures KAI KF-21 Boramae?
KAI KF-21 Boramae: Korea Aerospace Industries. The KAI KF-21 Boramae (Korean: KF-21 보라매; lit. 'KF-21 Hunting Hawk'; formerly KF-X; commonly KF-21) is a South Korean twin-engine fighter aircraft.
In which country did the Chengdu J-10 take place?

Chengdu J-10: People's Republic of China. It is produced by the Chengdu Aircraft Corporation (CAC) for the People's Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) of China, and exported to the Pakistan Air Force (PAF).
Who is credited with discovering Dubnium?
Dubnium: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. Dubnium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Db and atomic number 105.
Who is credited with discovering Brainfuck?
Brainfuck: Urban Müller. Brainfuck is an esoteric programming language created in 1993 by Swiss student Urban Müller.
Who is credited with discovering Cobalt?
Cobalt: Georg Brandt. Cobalt is a chemical element; it has symbol Co and atomic number 27.
Often confused with the unrelated sweet chestnut, this large deciduous tree in the maple, soapberry, and lychee family bears hermaphroditic flowers — what tree is it?
Aesculus hippocastanum is a species of flowering plant in the maple, soapberry and lychee family Sapindaceae.
A member of the aminopenicillin family usually swallowed by mouth, this go-to remedy for ear infections, strep throat, and pneumonia is often paired with clavulanic acid — which antibiotic is it?
Amoxicillin is an antibiotic medication belonging to the aminopenicillin class of the penicillin family.
The 16th-largest family of flowering plants, this aromatic group includes cumin, fennel, and coriander alongside deadly relatives like water hemlock — which family?
Apiaceae is a family of mostly aromatic flowering plants named after the type genus Apium, and commonly known as the celery, carrot, or parsley family, or simply as umbellifers.
These tiny prokaryotes fix nitrogen from the atmosphere, recycle nutrients, and handle the rotting of dead bodies — and they were among the very first life forms to appear on Earth. What are they?
Bacteria are ubiquitous, mostly free-living organisms often consisting of one biological cell.
Ranging from fingerprints and iris scans to typing rhythm and the way someone walks, these measurable human traits are used for identification and surveillance — what's the general term for them?
Biometrics are body measurements and calculations related to human characteristics and features.
Whose book Atlas of the Heart became an HBO Max documentary series in 2022, following an earlier Netflix film about her work on courage?
Brené Brown (born November 18, 1965) is an American academic, author and podcaster.
Prized in India for hashish and cultivated from China to West Africa, this Hindu Kush-native plant produces cannabinoid levels well above ordinary hemp — which species?
Cannabis indica is an annual plant species in the family Cannabaceae indigenous to the Hindu Kush mountains of Southern Asia.

A member of the poppy family found across Europe and western Asia, this herbaceous plant is nicknamed 'greater celandine' and isn't actually related to the similarly-named 'lesser celandine' — what's its scientific name?
Chelidonium majus is a perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the poppy family Papaveraceae.

Native to western South America, this shrub bears oval leaves and red berries, and when its leaves are chewed or brewed as tea they act as a mild stimulant with no evidence of addiction — which plant is it?
Coca refers to any of the four cultivated plants in the family Erythroxylaceae, native to western South America.
Belonging to the same genus as poliovirus and echovirus, these enteroviruses enter cells with help from a shared receptor and commonly cause aseptic meningitis — which pathogens?

Coxsackievirus are a few related enteroviruses that belong to the Picornaviridae family of nonenveloped, linear, positive-sense, single-stranded, RNA viruses, as well as its genus Enterovirus, which also includes poliovirus and echovirus.
Used to treat ADHD and narcolepsy, this 'right-handed' mirror-image form of a stimulant molecule is also misused to boost cognitive and athletic performance — what is it?
Dextroamphetamine is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant and enantiomer of amphetamine that is used in the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy.
This soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida is also known by slang names like 'dew-worm,' 'rainworm,' and 'nightcrawler.' What creature is it?
Earthworm is a soil-dwelling terrestrial invertebrate that belongs to the phylum Annelida.

This is the only living group of horses, asses, and zebras — odd-toed, herbivorous mammals whose ancestors first evolved in North America before spreading into Asia, Africa, and South America — what is it?
Equus (genus) is a genus of mammals in the perissodactyl family Equidae, which includes horses, asses, and zebras.
This intracellular protein buffers the body against both iron deficiency and iron overload, and small amounts leak into the blood where doctors measure it as a diagnostic marker — what protein is it?
Ferritin is a universal intracellular and extracellular protein that stores iron and releases it in a controlled fashion.

This genus of scented flowering shrubs in the coffee family was named for an 18th-century naturalist, though Carl Linnaeus gets most of the credit over the botanist who first proposed it — which genus?
Gardenia is a genus of flowering plants in the coffee family, Rubiaceae, native to the tropical and subtropical regions of Africa, Asia, Madagascar, Pacific Islands, and Australia.
This term describes the overall system of processes, rules, and power structures that sets boundaries of conduct and steers the direction of an organized group — what is it?

Governance is the overall complex system or framework of processes, functions, structures, rules, laws and norms born out of the relationships, interactions, power dynamics and communication within an organized group of individuals.

His synergy with information-theory father Claude Shannon laid foundations for the Information Age, and during WWII he helped build automatic guns that defended London from V-1 flying bombs — who was this Dutch-American control-theory pioneer?
Hendrik Wade Bode (-d,; December 24, 1905 - June 21, 1982) was an American engineer, researcher, inventor, author and scientist, of Dutch ancestry.
This thin piece of mucosal tissue that surrounds or partially covers the vaginal opening takes its name from a Greek word meaning 'thin skin' — name the structure?
Hymen is a thin piece of mucosal tissue that surrounds or partially covers the vaginal opening. It forms part of the vulva and is similar in structure to the vagina.
One of the largest dog breeds in the world, this sighthound was historically used to course game and became the official mascot of a British Guards regiment in 1902. What breed is it?
Irish Wolfhound is a breed of large sighthound that has, by its presence and substantial size, inspired literature, poetry and mythology.
Two years after unveiling the first mechanical television system, this Scottish engineer achieved the first-ever transatlantic television transmission in 1928 — who is he?
John Logie Baird (13 August 1888 - 14 June 1946) was a Scottish inventor, electrical engineer and innovator who demonstrated the world's first mechanical television system on 26 January 1926.
Named from the Greek word for 'the hidden one', this colorless, odorless noble gas with atomic number 36 is used in fluorescent lamps and high-powered gas lasers. Name the element?
Krypton (from Ancient) is a chemical element; it has symbol Kr and atomic number 36.

Named after the Italian word for lemon, this colorless liquid hydrocarbon is the main compound behind citrus peel fragrance, occurring mostly as a right-handed form extracted commercially by centrifugal separation or steam distillation - name the compound?

Limonene is a colorless liquid aliphatic hydrocarbon classified as a cyclic monoterpene, and is the major component in the fragrance and essential oil of citrus fruit peels, taking its name from Italian limone ("lemon").
This marsupial family native to Australia and New Guinea includes kangaroos, wallabies, quokkas, and tree-kangaroos among its 63 living species — what family is it?
Macropodidae is a family of marsupials that includes kangaroos, wallabies, tree-kangaroos, wallaroos, pademelons, the quokka, and several other groups.
Ranging from Patagonia to Bolivia during the Ice Age, this genus of giant ground sloths includes a type species that could weigh nearly four tonnes — which genus?

Megatherium (meg--; from Greek mga 'great' + theron 'beast') is an extinct genus of large ground sloths endemic to South America that lived from the Early Pliocene through the end of the Late Pleistocene.
By dividing one cell into two with an identical set of chromosomes apiece, this stage of the cell cycle keeps genetic stability intact across generations — what is it?
Mitosis is a part of the cell cycle in eukaryotic cells in which replicated chromosomes are separated into two new nuclei.
A white crystalline solid built from two fused benzene rings, this aromatic compound is the main ingredient of traditional mothballs and has an odor you can smell at just 0.08 ppm. What is it?
Naphthalene is an organic compound with the chemical formula C10H8.
What's the name for the scholarly study and collection of coins, paper money, tokens and medals — though by its rules, cigarettes traded in prison don't count?
Numismatics is the study or collection of currency, including coins, tokens, paper money, medals, and related objects.
Jointly built by Italy, the UK and Germany, this variable-sweep-wing combat aircraft comes in strike, electronic-warfare and interceptor variants — which jet?
Panavia Tornado is a family of twin-engine, variable-sweep wing multi-role combat aircraft, jointly developed and manufactured by Italy, the United Kingdom and Germany.
This class of compounds is defined by a direct single bond between two oxygen atoms, denoted R−O−O−R — what are they called?
Peroxide are a group of molecules with the structure ROOR, where each R represents a radical (a portion of a complete molecule; not a free radical) and the O's are single oxygen atoms.
In Aristotle's day this kingdom included algae and fungi, but modern definitions have narrowed it to chiefly photosynthetic, mostly multicellular organisms — what is it?
Plant are the eukaryotic organisms that constitute the kingdom Plantae.

This endogenous steroid sex hormone plays a central role in the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and embryonic development, and also serves as a key metabolic intermediate for producing other steroid hormones — name the hormone?
Progesterone (P4) is an endogenous steroid and progestogen sex hormone involved in the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and embryogenesis of humans and other species.

Cultivated mainly for its oil-rich seeds, this yellow-flowered Brassica crop is the source of a low-toxicity oil marketed under a Canadian-coined name, and ranks as the world's third-largest vegetable oil source — what is it?
Caused by two strains of human herpesvirus and nicknamed 'sixth disease,' this common childhood illness brings a rapid fever that gives way to a pink rash within days — what's it called?
Roseola is an infectious disease caused by certain types of human herpes viruses.
With segmented bony armor, an upright posture, and a curling prehensile tail, these 46 species of tiny bony fish are cousins to the pipefishes and seadragons — what are they?
Seahorse (also written sea-horse and sea horse) is any of 46 species of small marine bony fish in the genus Hippocampus.
Whether on land, in fresh water, or in the sea, this gastropod earns its name from a coiled shell roomy enough to fully retract into — what is it?
Snail is a shelled gastropod. The name is most often applied to land snails, terrestrial pulmonate gastropod molluscs.

In 1976, this American engineer and inventor co-founded Apple Computer with his early business partner, later becoming known as one of the personal computer revolution's most important pioneers — who is he?
Steve Wozniak (born August 11, 1950), also known by his nickname Woz, is an American technology entrepreneur, electrical engineer, computer programmer, and inventor.
Every part of this Old World evergreen tree is poisonous except the fleshy red covering around its seed, and it's native across Eurasia and Northwest Africa — what tree species is it?
Taxus baccata is an Old World species of evergreen tree in the family Taxaceae.
Tetrapods have these digits at the end of each limb; horses walk on their very tips in what's called an unguligrade stance — what are they?
Toe are the digits of the foot of a tetrapod.
Native to cool climates across the Northern Hemisphere, this low shrub bears small, round, edible fruit of a deep blue color, and goes by several folk names depending on region — what's the species?
Vaccinium myrtillus is a holarctic species of shrub with edible fruit of blue color, known by the common names bilberry, blaeberry, and whortleberry.
The first-ever recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physics, this German scientist discovered a form of electromagnetic radiation named after him in some languages — who was he?

Wilhelm Röntgen (27 March 1845 - 10 February 1923) was a German experimental physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays (known as Rntgen rays in many languages).
This Andalusi polymath built a model of the planets' motion, devised colourless glass, made reading lenses, and is even said to have attempted flight — who was this 9th-century inventor?
Abbas ibn Firnas: 9th-century astronomer and physician.
People with this anxiety disorder dread places they feel they can't safely escape — crowds, queues, public transit — and in severe cases become unable to leave home at all. What is it?
Agoraphobia: Anxiety disorder. Agoraphobia is believed to be due to a combination of genetic and environmental factors.
A succulent from the Arabian Peninsula, this popular potted plant stores a soothing gel of acemannan in its leaves — alongside a toxic compound called aloin. What is it?
Aloe vera: Species of plant. It is widely distributed, and is considered an invasive species in many world regions.

Born in Dunfermline, Scotland, and immigrating to Pittsburgh at age 12, this steel magnate gave away nearly 90 percent of his fortune after publishing an 1889 essay called 'The Gospel of Wealth' — who is he?
Andrew Carnegie: American industrialist and philanthropist (1835–1919)
In this severe blood disorder, the bone marrow stops producing red cells, white cells and platelets alike, and about half of all cases have no known cause — what condition is it?
Aplastic anemia: Disease causing insufficient blood cells of all types.

One of its founders, James Keeler, said this science 'seeks to ascertain the nature of the heavenly bodies... rather than their positions or motions' — studying everything from the Sun to the cosmic microwave background. What field is it?
Sitting at the bottom of the forebrain and including the striatum and substantia nigra, this cluster of brain nuclei governs voluntary movement and habit formation — what is it called?
Basal ganglia: Group of subcortical nuclei involved in the motor and reward systems.
This field covers physiological traits like fingerprints and iris patterns, plus behavioral ones like typing rhythm and gait, all used to identify people — what is it called?
Biometrics: Metrics related to human characteristics.

Despite lacking the tight head of typical cabbage, this leafy Chinese vegetable has a flavor often compared to spinach and water chestnuts, with a milder white bulb and stronger-tasting green leaves — what vegetable is it?
Bok choy: Subspecies of flowering plant.
With a large head, deep facial folds, and a flat face with a jutting lower jaw, this British breed's ancestors were once used for baiting cattle before the sport was banned in 1835 — which breed?
Bulldog: British breed of dog. It may also be known as the English Bulldog or British Bulldog.
First classified by Linnaeus in 1753 and indigenous to Eastern Asia, this annual flowering plant has been cultivated throughout history for fiber, oil, food, and medicine — which plant?
Cannabis sativa: Plant species. It has been cultivated throughout recorded history and used as a source of industrial fiber, seed oil, food, and medicine.

Named from a Latin word meaning 'blind,' this pouch at the start of the large intestine sits on the same side of the body as the appendix and receives chyme straight from the small intestine — which structure?
Cecum: Pouch in the large intestine. It is typically located on the right side of the body (the same side of the body as the appendix, to which it is joined).

First recorded in the 3rd-to-5th-century manuscript Sunzi Suanjing, this number-theory result lets you deduce what's left over after dividing by a product of coprime numbers, just from the leftovers after dividing by each one — which principle?
Chinese remainder theorem: About simultaneous modular congruences.
This genus of anaerobic, Gram-positive bacteria found in soil and animal intestines includes the microbes responsible for both botulism and tetanus — which genus?
Clostridium: Genus of bacteria. Species of Clostridium inhabit soils and the intestinal tracts of animals, including humans.
Named from ancient Greek for 'footless' after being mistaken for a legless swallow, this bird's closest relatives are actually hummingbirds — and it almost never touches the ground. Which bird?
Common swift: Species of bird. The resemblances between the groups are due to convergent evolution, reflecting similar contextual development.
Found in the tropics of Africa, Asia, the Americas, and Australia, this large semiaquatic reptile congregates in rivers and wetlands and is closely related to alligators and caimans — what is it?
Crocodile: Family of large reptilian carnivores.
In 1900, this mathematician presented a list of unsolved problems that shaped 20th-century mathematical research — who is he?
This linguistic term describes a combination of two vowel sounds gliding together within a single syllable, as heard five times in the phrase 'no highway cowboys' — what is it called?

Diphthong: Combination of two adjacent vowel sounds. A diphthong ( DIF-thong, DIP-), also known as a gliding vowel or a vowel glide, is a combination of two adjacent vowel sounds within the same syllable.
Named after the Greek word for 'hedgehog' because of its spiky central disk, this North American daisy relative is nicknamed the coneflower — what is it?
Echinacea: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family.
Builder of the world's first artificial nuclear reactor, Chicago Pile-1, this Manhattan Project physicist won the 1938 Nobel for work with slow neutrons — who was he?
Grey-buff to pinkish-grey with a black half-collar edged in white, this bird species native to Europe, Asia, and North Africa has also been introduced to Japan and the Americas. What is it?
Eurasian collared dove: Species of bird. The Eurasian collared dove (Streptopelia decaocto), often just collared dove, is a dove species.
Native to North African deserts from Western Sahara to the Sinai, this diminutive canid uses its oversized ears to shed heat and detect prey burrowing underground — which species is it?
Fennec fox: Species of fox. The fennec fox (Vulpes zerda) is a small fox native to the deserts of North Africa, ranging from Western Sahara and Mauritania to the Sinai Peninsula.
A pungent colorless gas churned out at 26 million tons a year, it's used to make resins and, in a roughly 37% solution, to preserve tissue samples in labs — what is it?

Marked by heartburn, regurgitation, and even dental corrosion from stomach acid creeping back up the digestive tract, this chronic condition can, if untreated, lead to esophageal stricture or Barrett's esophagus — what is it?
Gastroesophageal reflux disease: Flow of stomach contents into the esophagus.
Produced by the pancreas's alpha cells, this hormone raises blood sugar by triggering the liver to break down stored glycogen — the functional opposite of insulin. What is it?
Glucagon: Peptide hormone. It raises the concentration of glucose and fatty acids in the bloodstream and is considered to be the main catabolic hormone of the body.
Credited as the inventor of radio, this Italian engineer shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics and later set up Vatican Radio for Pope Pius XI — who is he?
Guglielmo Marconi: Italian radio-frequency engineer and inventor (1874–1937)
Native to Africa south of the Sahara, this domesticated bird has since been introduced everywhere from the West Indies to Australia — which species?
Helmeted guinea fowl: Species of bird. The helmeted guinea fowl (Numida meleagris) is the best known of the guinea fowl bird family, Numididae, and the only member of the genus Numida.
Also called the ratel, this remarkably loose-skinned mammal — able to twist freely inside its own hide — is the largest land member of the weasel family in Africa. What is it?
Honey badger: Species of mammal. The honey badger (Mellivora capensis), also known as the ratel ( or), is a mammal widely distributed across Africa, Southwest Asia, and the Indian subcontinent.

Diagnosed via Whipple's triad and most often triggered by diabetes medications like insulin, this condition causes shakiness, confusion, and sweating when blood sugar drops below 70 mg/dL — what is it?

Hypoglycemia: Decrease in blood sugar. It is defined as blood glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), symptoms associated with hypoglycemia, and resolution of symptoms when blood sugar returns to normal.
Most often extracted from chicory, this plant-stored fructan earned FDA approval as a dietary fiber in 2018 and remains the gold-standard compound for measuring kidney filtration rates — what is it?
A Communist Party member and Stanford-trained psychiatrist, this woman is best remembered for her romantic relationship with J. Robert Oppenheimer, which put her under FBI surveillance. Who is she?
Personal physician to the Buddha and King Bimbisāra in 5th-century BCE Rājagṛha, this 'Medicine King' is still revered by traditional healers across Asia — who is he?

Jīvaka: Personal physician of the Buddha and Indian King Bimbisara. Jīvaka (Pali: Jīvaka Komārabhacca; Sanskrit: Jīvaka Kaumārabhṛtya) was the personal physician (Sanskrit: vaidya) of the Buddha and the Indian King Bimbisāra.
What is this — “Parts of the vulva”?
Labia: Parts of the vulva. The labia are the major externally visible structures of the vulva.
Used to treat everything from pneumonia to Legionnaires' disease, this broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibiotic is the left-handed mirror-image isomer of a drug called ofloxacin — what is it?
Levofloxacin: Antibiotic. Levofloxacin, sold under the brand name Levaquin among others, is a broad-spectrum antibiotic of the fluoroquinolone drug class.
Sometimes called the Japanese medlar or Japanese plum, this evergreen tree from the hills of south-central China produces small orange fruit — which plant?
Loquat: Species of plant. The loquat (Eriobotrya japonica, Chinese: 枇杷; Pinyin: pípá) is a large evergreen shrub or tree grown commercially for its orange coloured fruits.
Genetically related to the Bichon, Bolognese, and Havanese, this toy breed sports a silky white coat, doesn't shed, and tops out around 4 kilograms — what breed is it?
Maltese dog: Breed of toy dog. The precise link, if any, between the modern and ancient breeds is not known.

Entering US Navy service in 1961 before the Marines and Air Force adopted it too, this twin-engine supersonic jet became America's most-produced supersonic military aircraft with 5,195 built — which aircraft?
McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II: Fighter aircraft family developed from 1958.
Sold as Flagyl, this antibiotic and antiprotozoal fights everything from giardiasis to trichomoniasis — but it's notorious for leaving a metallic taste in your mouth — what is it?
Metronidazole: Antibiotic and antiprotozoal medication. Metronidazole, sold under the brand name Flagyl and Metrogyl among others, is an antibiotic and antiprotozoal medication.
Its dust-like, colored, fuzzy appearance on food comes from spores, and its branching network of hyphae — called a mycelium — counts as a single organism; what fungal structure is this?
Mold: Wooly, dust-like fungal structure or substance.
This symbiotic partnership between fungus and plant roots plays a crucial role in plant nutrition and soil chemistry — usually mutualistic, but sometimes parasitic. What's the association called?
Mycorrhiza: Fungus-plant symbiotic association. The term mycorrhiza refers to the role of the fungus in the plant's rhizosphere, the plant root system and its surroundings.

This silvery-white transition metal with a faint golden tinge resists corrosion thanks to a thin oxide layer, and in pure native form it's mostly found inside iron meteorites — which element, atomic number 28, is it?
Nickel: Chemical element with atomic number 28 (Ni)

This family within the superfamily Delphinoidea includes species with 'whale' in their common names, like the pilot and false killer types, and ranges up in size to the massive orca — what is this family called?
Oceanic dolphin: Family of marine mammals.
This genus of highly sociable ruminants includes domestic sheep, believed to descend from the wild mouflon of central and southwest Asia — which genus?
Ovis: Genus of mammals. Ovis is a genus of mammals, part of the Caprinae subfamily of the ruminant family Bovidae.
He earned a PhD in physics from Cambridge for the first-ever thesis on quantum mechanics, then shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Erwin Schrödinger — who is he?
Known on the street as 'angel dust,' this dissociative anesthetic acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist and can cause hallucinations and psychosis — what is this drug?
Phencyclidine: Dissociative hallucinogenic drug, mostly used recreationally.

Commonly known as plantains or fleaworts — though unrelated to the banana-like cooking fruit of the same name — this genus of roughly 200 mostly herbaceous flowering plants tops out around 24 inches tall. Which genus?
Plantago: Genus of flowering plants. Plantago is a genus of about 200 species of flowering plants in the family Plantaginaceae, commonly called plantains or fleaworts.
This glucocorticoid medication used to suppress the immune system is actually a prodrug that the liver must convert into its active form before it works — what is it?
Prednisone: Steroid medication. It is also used to treat high blood calcium due to cancer and adrenal insufficiency along with other corticosteroids.
Often starting as a blood clot in the leg that travels to the lungs, this blockage can cause chest pain on breathing in, coughing up blood, and sudden death — what is the condition?

Pulmonary embolism: Blockage of an artery in the lungs. Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a blockage of an artery in the lungs by a substance that has moved from elsewhere in the body through the bloodstream (embolism).
